ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Transplant rejection is an immune attack against donor tissue, leading to graft dysfunction. It is classified by timing, mechanism, and severity, guiding therapy and monitoring.

sections.p: Rejection occurs when recipient immune cells recognize donor antigens as foreign, triggering inflammation and tissue injury. Diagnosis combines clinical signs, graft function tests, and biopsy confirmation.

t.b: ↑ indicates impaired function, prompting further workup
Findings: interface dermatitis, necrosis, lymphocytic infiltrate

sections.p: Rejection is staged by organ-specific criteria, reflecting histologic grade and functional decline. Early stages may be reversible; late stages often irreversible.

t.b: Grade I mild, Grade III severe

sections.p: The primary driver is alloimmune T-cell activation. Other contributors include infections, drug toxicity, and non‑adherence to immunosuppression.

t.b: Treat infection to reduce immune activation

sections.p: Symptoms mirror graft dysfunction: fever, pain, swelling, or organ-specific signs such as oliguria, jaundice, or skin rash.
Workup includes functional labs, imaging if needed, and definitive biopsy. When resources are limited, clinical judgment and basic labs guide management.
Rapid graft loss, sepsis, or multi‑organ failure are life‑threatening. Early recognition and treatment are critical.
Treat by intensifying immunosuppression, addressing infections, and supporting organ function. Choice of drugs balances efficacy, toxicity, and drug interactions.
Regular monitoring of drug levels, graft function, and antibody screens prevents rejection. Patient education on adherence is essential.
Infections, drug toxicity, and surgical complications can mimic rejection.
Low drug levels may be falsely normal if assay errors occur; mild elevations in liver enzymes can be due to hepatitis rather than rejection.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden graft dysfunction, high fever, severe pain, or signs of sepsis

faq.a: Acute cellular rejection, driven by T-cell activation.
